Path hiding

In the basic protocol, each client submits its histogram vector only for its current tree node. The shares themselves reveal nothing, but the node tag accompanying them does: shareholders learn which leaf the client occupies, and hence its tree path. For medical data, this can be sensitive-e.g., a shareholder learns that a patient's glucose exceeds a diagnostic threshold.

Path hiding eliminates this leakage. Instead of submitting a vector for only its true node, each client submits vectors for all active leaf nodes in the current treebuilding iteration (Fig. 3). For the true node, the client shares its actual histogram vector. For all other nodes, it shares an all-zero vector. Since Shamir shares of zero are indistinguishable from shares of any other value, a coalition of fewer than m shareholders cannot distinguish the client's true node from the shared vectors alone.

For the same participating records and training decisions, adding secret-shared zero contributions for unoccupied nodes leaves the reconstructed aggregates unchanged. Path hiding therefore preserves the resulting model under these conditions. The cost is communication overhead: in tree-building iteration ℓ, each client submits vectors for |V ℓ | ≤ 2 ℓ active nodes instead of one (quantified in "Communication cost" in Results). This mechanism is captured by the loop over active leaf nodes in Algorithm 1. Disabling path hiding reduces to submitting shares only for v * i.

Security analysis

PrivateBoost protects individual contributions during aggregation using threshold secret sharing. We analyse an honest-but-curious setting in which parties follow the protocol but may attempt to infer private information from their observations. We consider the aggregator, a coalition of fewer than m shareholders, and a coalition of clients separately. The analysis does not cover coalitions combining these roles or parties that deviate from the prescribed computation. This analysis identifies information exposed by the protocol and potential attack mechanisms; it does not empirically evaluate attack effectiveness. Each client distributes its encoded contribution among n shareholders using Shamir secret sharing. With independently and uniformly sampled polynomial coefficients, any collection of fewer than m shares has a joint distribution independent of the shared value [21]. This property applies separately to every entry of the feature-statistics and gradient-Hessian vectors. Shareholders can therefore add their shares without recovering individual contributions, while the aggregator reconstructs sums from the responses of m shareholders. The information-theoretic property concerns the mathematical sharing scheme; its implementation uses a pseudorandom generator to sample coefficients.

The reconstruction threshold determines the tolerated shareholder collusion. Our default 2-of-3 configuration protects individual shares against one curious shareholder, whereas 3-of-5 protects against coalitions of up to two. A coalition of m shareholders can reconstruct an individual contribution. Aggregation requires the selected shareholders to hold submissions from a common cohort of at least k min clients; subject to this condition, up to n -m shareholders may be unavailable. Increasing n at fixed m provides more choices of an available shareholder subset but does not raise the collusion threshold. Increasing m strengthens collusion resistance while requiring more shareholder responses. Each client sends shares to all n shareholders, so increasing their number also increases communication.

Table 6 reports the measured costs of both configurations.

Protection of the numerical shares does not conceal all information associated with a submission. Each shareholder observes persistent client pseudonyms and can link participation across rounds. In the base protocol, node tags also reveal the client's current tree node and hence its path through the tree. Individual feature-bin assignments are not transmitted as metadata: each histogram contains shares for every bin, including shares of zero for unoccupied positions. Under the shareholder threshold assumption, these shares do not distinguish occupied from empty bins beyond information available from the visible metadata. Path hiding extends this construction to every active node, so node tags no longer identify the client's actual node. It does not conceal participation, persistent pseudonyms or transport metadata.

The aggregator receives aggregate outputs rather than individual contribution shares. During the statistics phase, these outputs comprise feature and label sums, their squared-value sums, and the contributing record count. They disclose population summaries, including feature means and the prevalence of the positive label in the cohort. These are intended outputs, but may still be sensitive. During training, the aggregator receives gradient and Hessian sums for each active node and feature bin. It also observes round commitments, their delivery across shareholders and the selected shareholder set. Fresh nonces make commitments vary across rounds, but do not hide the delivery pattern within a round. Clients receive the bin edges, initial ensemble score, split decisions and updated ensemble, including leaf values.

Small node or bin populations can expose individual information within these aggregates. The minimum-client threshold applies to the common contributing cohort, not to occupancy within each node or bin. Although bin counts are not separately released, they can sometimes be recovered from the Hessian sums. Under binary logistic loss with a common predicted probability of 0.5, each record contributes a Hessian of 0.25, making the bin count four times its Hessian sum. If that count is one, the gradient g i = 0.5 -y i also reveals the record's binary label: +0.5 corresponds to y i = 0 and -0.5 to y i = 1. Associating the recovered label with a particular person requires additional information. Contributions disclosed by colluding clients could likewise be subtracted from an aggregate, potentially isolating another client's contribution; such mixed coalitions are outside the analysis.

Repeated releases create further opportunities for inference. If two aggregates contain identical contributions from the same records except for one, their difference reveals that record's contribution even when both cohorts exceed k min . Changing gradients and unknown cohort overlap complicate this subtraction, and attributing the result to an individual requires further information. Lam et al. demonstrated disaggregation of federated updates using repeated aggregates and participation summary analytics, assuming an adversarial server that can hold the model fixed across rounds [26]. This motivates considering releases jointly. Controls on repeated aggregation requests and cohort selection could limit opportunities for deliberate isolation, but a minimum cohort size alone does not protect against inference across releases.

Secure aggregation therefore limits direct access to individual gradients without establishing protection against reconstruction from released statistics or membership inference from trained models. Gradient reconstruction and membership inference have been demonstrated in neural-network settings [27, 28]. Differential privacy offers complementary protection by limiting the influence of an individual record on released information and has been applied to federated boosted trees [16]. An extension would need bounded contributions, calibrated noise and privacy accounting across the statistics phase and subsequent training releases. Protection against the aggregator would require perturbation before it observes the sums. PrivateBoost does not currently implement differential privacy.

Malicious behaviour introduces risks beyond this semi-honest analysis. A coordinator could attempt to isolate contributions by manipulating cohort selection or providing different training contexts to different clients. Pasquini et al. demonstrated model-inconsistency attacks against secure aggregation in federated neural-network training [29]. Verifiable agreement on the training context and enforceable aggregation rules would be relevant safeguards. If enrolment permits an attacker to register multiple client identities, those identities could dominate a cohort, distort training or facilitate subtraction using their known contributions. The client-count threshold does not establish that participants are independent people. Enrolment controls would address this concern, while validation of contribution bounds and histogram structure would address malformed submissions. These safeguards would require separate design and evaluation; the current analysis establishes neither resistance to malicious coordination nor protection against multiple attacker-controlled identities. Contribution validation and attestation are discussed further in the Discussion.

Communication and computation cost

We give bounds for single-record clients. Let c denote the number of clients, n the number of shareholders, m the reconstruction threshold, F the number of features, T the number of trees, and d the maximum number of tree-building iterations. Let V t,ℓ denote the current leaves considered in iteration ℓ of tree t, taking this set to be empty for iterations omitted by early stopping. There are B These expressions describe histogram traffic and the associated sharing, reconstruction and split-finding work. They exclude commitment exchange, shareholder selection, HTTP framing, polling and delivery of the model and round context; they do not represent total client computation. The current selection routine enumerates the n m shareholder subsets and compares their commitment intersections; its cost matters when increasing the shareholder population. For fixed m, client sharing costs grow linearly with n, while aggregate reconstruction uses only m shareholders. More shareholders provide additional choices of an available subset, provided that subset has a sufficiently large common contributing cohort. Raising m improves collusion resistance but increases sharing and reconstruction costs. For fixed model and shareholder parameters, each single-record client's histogram payload and sharing work are bounded independently of the total client population. "Communication cost" and "Real-world deployment" report measured traffic and device-side costs.

Experimental setup

We evaluate whether privacy-preserving aggregation from single-record clients can match the predictive quality of centralised training across four structured medical classification tasks of increasing scale. Three small datasets long distributed by the UCI Machine Learning Repository represent common diagnostic scenarios: Heart Disease [30, 31] (Cleveland subset, 297 of 303 records retained after excluding those with missing values, 13 features), Breast Cancer [32, 33] (569 samples, 30 features, analysed from the copy bundled with scikit-learn), and Pima Diabetes [34, 35] (768 samples, 8 features). To evaluate predictive performance with a larger simulated population of single-record clients, we additionally use the CDC Diabetes Health Indicators dataset as distributed by UCI [36]. From the 253,680 records of that release we draw a classbalanced subset of 70,692 samples, comprising all 35,346 records labelled positive in the binary target together with an equal-sized random sample of negative cases, over 21 health indicator features predicting the combined prediabetes-or-diabetes binary target. In the predictive-performance simulations, each client holds exactly one training record, the regime in which a patient contributes a single diagnostic measurement from a personal device. We report results over 5 stratified random 80/20 train/test splits (mean ± std).

The evaluations use three distinct client configurations. Predictive-performance simulations assign one training record to each client. Loopback communication measurements use one single-record client and one batch client. The physical pilot uses four smartphones and tablets, each holding a batch, with the server roles co-located. The minimum-client threshold is separate from the Shamir reconstruction threshold: the simulation executable defaults to k min = 10; the loopback session requires two clients, with shareholder release floors set to one for functional measurement; and the pilot configuration sets both the session minimum and shareholder release floor to three devices. These thresholds apply to the common contributing cohort, not to the number of nonzero contributions in each node or bin.

We use a 2-of-3 Shamir threshold, 10 bins per feature, max depth 3, 15 trees, learning rate 0.15, regularisation λ = 2.0, and logistic loss. Bin edges are placed at Gaussian quantile boundaries as described in "Protocol flow". We compare against two XGBoost baselines: (1) XGBoost with matched tree hyperparameters (depth, trees, learning rate, λ, and 10 bins), and (2) XGBoost with default settings.

Results

Model quality

PrivateBoost achieved predictive performance comparable to matched centralised XGBoost across the four evaluated datasets (Fig. 4). The learning curves overlap or closely track the matched configuration, typically reaching their final AUC-ROC within 8-10 trees.

Table 2 reports final classification metrics. PrivateBoost and matched XGBoost have the same mean accuracy on Heart Disease and CDC BRFSS (81.7% and 74.2%, respectively). Their mean AUC-ROC values are 0.880 and 0.879 on Heart Disease, respectively, and both are 0.818 on CDC BRFSS. Mean AUC-ROC is also similar on Breast Cancer (0.985 versus 0.984) and Pima Diabetes (0.841 versus 0.835). The default XGBoost configuration achieves a higher mean AUC-ROC of 0.826 on CDC BRFSS.

Binning analysis

In the evaluated implementation, PrivateBoost derives histogram boundaries from aggregate feature means and variances. These boundaries determine the candidate split thresholds available during training. We compare two strategies: Gaussian quantile binning, which places edges at equal-probability quantiles of N (µ, σ 2 ), and equal-width binning, which spaces edges at equal intervals across the same range.

Fig. 5 illustrates the mechanisms on two continuous Pima Diabetes features. On near-symmetric Glucose (γ1 = 0.17), Gaussian quantile binning distributes bin edges more evenly across the data-dense region. On the heavily skewed Insulin feature (γ1 = 2.27), both methods concentrate approximately 49% of samples in a single bin due to a zero-inflated spike, limiting the resolution of either approach.

Bin boundaries could also be specified using prior knowledge or an independent reference dataset. For example, established clinical thresholds for a blood test could define candidate split points without estimating them from participating clients' records. The protocol would then aggregate gradients and Hessians within these predefined bins and select splits using the same gain criterion. The usefulness of such boundaries would depend on their relevance to the target population and prediction task.

Client dropout resilience

Intermittent client availability can affect both bin estimation and tree construction. We evaluate three failure modes separately: dropout during gradient rounds, dropout during the one-time statistics phase, and loss of individual client-to-shareholder submissions. Aggregation can proceed when m shareholders hold contributions from a common cohort of at least k min clients. The selected shareholders sum shares from that same cohort, ensuring consistent reconstruction despite missing submissions. The Shamir threshold m determines how many shareholder responses are required; k min determines the minimum contributing cohort size and does not ensure minimum occupancy in individual nodes or bins. The following experiments assess predictive performance under randomly sampled failures.

Gradient-round dropout. We randomly exclude a fraction of clients each gradient round, with independent sampling per round. Mean AUC-ROC remains close to or above the no-dropout baseline on Heart Disease, Breast Cancer and CDC BRFSS at 80-90% dropout (Fig. 6). Pima Diabetes shows a modest reduction, from 0.841 without dropout to 0.828 and 0.831 at 80% and 90% dropout, respectively. Variation across training splits does not increase consistently across datasets. Because clients are resampled each round, records excluded from one round can contribute later; these results do not represent permanent loss of the same clients or dropout correlated with their records.

Statistics-phase dropout. Table 5 reports AUC-ROC when bin edges are derived from a random subset of clients. Mean AUC-ROC remained close to the no-failure baseline at statistics-phase dropout rates of up to 90%. These results suggest that the aggregate mean and variance estimates were sufficient for binning in the evaluated settings. Per-shareholder message loss. Instead of removing whole clients, each clientto-shareholder submission is lost independently with probability q in every round. This exercises the consistency mechanism described in "Building blocks": the aggregator selects the m shareholders whose received commitment sets have the largest intersection, and a client whose submission missed any of the selected shareholders is excluded from that round's aggregate. Under this message-loss model, matching the contributing cohort prevents partial delivery from producing inconsistent aggregate shares; a round can proceed only if the common cohort meets the participation threshold. For any fixed pair of shareholders, q = 0.5 gives a contribution a (1-q)2 = 0.25 probability of reaching both; selecting the pair with the largest common cohort can retain more clients. In the evaluated 2-of-3 configuration, mean AUC-ROC decreases by at most 0.009 at q = 0.5 (Table 5), consistent with the gradient-round dropout results above.

Communication cost

We measured per-client communication using the complete protocol with clients, shareholders and aggregator running on the same computer and communicating through the local loopback interface. Measurements cover all four datasets, both Shamir thresholds and both path-hiding settings. One client holds a single record, while a second holds the remaining dataset records as a batch. In each gradient round, clients send each shareholder a batch containing a commitment, routing information and histogram shares for their current node or, with path hiding, all active nodes. We record the single-record client's total bytes sent and received at the TCP-stream interface, including TLS handshakes, HTTP/2 framing, submissions and round-context polling. These measurements provide a controlled comparison of per-client traffic across protocol configurations. The physical-device pilot below evaluates participation and submission costs during mobile background execution. Without path hiding, total per-client traffic under the 2-of-3 configuration ranges from 586 KiB for Pima Diabetes to 1,368 KiB for Breast Cancer (Table 6). Traffic includes both submitted shares and downloaded round context: for CDC BRFSS, downloads account for approximately 222 KiB of the 1,056 KiB total. Moving to 3-of-Path hiding increases traffic because each client submits histogram shares for every active node at a depth level. A fully expanded depth-three tree requires contributions for 1 + 2 +4 = 7 nodes, compared with three node contributions without path hiding, giving a histogram-payload ratio of 7/3 ≈ 2.33. Actual overhead depends on the number of active nodes and is reduced in the total traffic by shared costs such as statistics collection and round-context downloads.

Increasing tree depth raises communication costs, particularly with path hiding, while predictive gains vary by dataset (Fig. 7). Pima Diabetes improves mainly up to depth three, CDC BRFSS continues to improve at greater depths, and Heart Disease and Breast Cancer show no consistent improvement across the tested depths. These results support depth three as a practical compromise between predictive performance and communication cost.

Real-world deployment

We evaluated whether consumer smartphones and tablets could complete training through background execution without user interaction after enrolment. The deployment used operating-system-managed execution opportunities to compute and submit contributions while device screens remained off.

Clients used silent push notifications and scheduled background tasks to obtain execution opportunities. The aggregator sent at most one silent notification per device every 15 minutes while a training round was open. Clients also registered background tasks through WorkManager on Android and background app refresh on iOS. Execution depended on operating-system scheduling; the configured notification interval did not guarantee when a device would run.

An aggregator and three shareholders using a 2-of-3 Shamir threshold ran on one cloud server with 2 vCPUs and 4 GB RAM, with client connections protected by TLS. Four consumer devices-a Google Pixel 9 Pro, Samsung Galaxy Tab A8, Lenovo Tab M8 and Apple iPhone 13 Pro-each held one quarter of every training set. Heart Disease, Pima Diabetes and Breast Cancer sessions ran concurrently overnight, each training eight trees of maximum depth three. Submission windows lasted up to one hour, with each round closing once three devices had contributed. We recorded model quality, contribution timing and triggers, computation and submission times, resident memory and network traffic.

All three training sessions completed within six hours and seventeen minutes without a failed round (Figure 8). Final test AUC-ROC was 0.933 for Heart Disease, 0.821 for Pima Diabetes and 0.997 for Breast Cancer (Figure 9a).

Remote wakeups triggered 223 of the 300 device contributions, and scheduled background tasks triggered the remaining 77. The Lenovo tablet relied almost entirely on scheduled tasks (Figure 10a). On every device, the median interval between successive submitted rounds within a session was 15.0 minutes, matching the configured notification interval (Figure 10b).

Across devices, median share-generation times ranged from 0.3 to 1.0 milliseconds per round, and median submission times from 116 to 149 milliseconds over TLS. Fig. 8: Timeline of the deployment. Each marker is one submitted round of the three concurrently trained sessions on the four devices; colour indicates the session, shape the wake trigger. Time is measured from the first submitted round of the capture. Median application resident memory ranged from 76 to 234 MB (Table 7). Accumulated share-generation and submission time was 9.1-12.4 seconds per device across the three sessions. Measured per-client traffic was 0.63-1.55 MB per session (Figure 9b).

The pilot demonstrates unattended training participation from consumer smartphones and tablets after one-tap enrolment per dataset. Computation and submission occupied only a small fraction of the elapsed training time, which was dominated by intervals between background execution opportunities. Battery consumption and perceived impact on device use were not measured. Table 7: On-device cost of participating in the deployment. Perdevice medians over all submitted rounds (n = 75 rounds per device, across the three concurrent sessions). Discussion

PrivateBoost enables clients to contribute individual records to gradient-boosted tree training without fitting local models or coordinating with other clients. The simulations show predictive performance comparable to matched centralised training, while the physical pilot demonstrates unattended participation from consumer smartphones and tablets holding batches of records. In the pilot, computation and submission occupied only a small fraction of the elapsed training time. Under the evaluated notification and participation schedule, intervals between background execution opportunities dominated completion time, highlighting the importance of the interactions required from each client. Clients can submit independently within a round, but training still follows the sequential dependencies of boosting. Each depth level depends on the preceding split decisions, and each tree uses predictions from the preceding ensemble. PrivateBoost accommodates changing participation between these rounds rather than requiring the same clients to remain available throughout training. The dropout experiments indicate that predictive performance can tolerate substantial randomly sampled nonparticipation in the evaluated datasets. In deployment, however, availability may correlate with device characteristics or participant behaviour, changing which records contribute and potentially introducing bias.

The use of external shareholders allows clients to finish their contribution to a round once their shares have been delivered. In Bonawitz et al.'s secure aggregation protocol, clients also participate in an unmasking phase after masked contributions have been collected. Individual clients may drop out after uploading, provided enough others supply the masking shares needed to complete aggregation [22]. These additional interactions may span multiple background execution windows. PrivateBoost can instead complete aggregation without further client responses once the selected shareholders hold a sufficiently large common set of contributions.

This design requires available shareholders and the stated limits on collusion. Client-based secure aggregation avoids the need for a fixed external shareholder set, and sparse-neighbourhood approaches reduce communication for coordination among clients [23]. With a fixed model configuration and shareholder set, PrivateBoost keeps each single-record client's contribution workload independent of the client population, while infrastructure workload grows with participation. The four-device pilot establishes background participation with locally batched records and co-located server roles. Evaluating concurrent connections, polling and aggregation across independently operated shareholders would extend these findings to larger populations. Matched workloads and participation schedules would also allow the completion times of the two aggregation architectures to be compared.

The privacy guarantees concern both the numerical contributions and the information exposed by their submission. Threshold secret sharing protects individual contributions from coalitions of fewer than m shareholders, and path hiding conceals the node membership otherwise revealed by selective submissions. The aggregator nevertheless receives exact statistics, and the trained model also remains available for analysis. Gradient-reconstruction and membership-inference attacks illustrate how information about training records can be recovered from gradients or learned models [27, 28]. Although those studies examine neural-network settings, the distinction between protecting individual messages and protecting released information also applies here. Small node or bin populations can make aggregate outputs particularly revealing.

Differential privacy offers complementary protection by limiting the influence of an individual record on released information [37]. Maddock et al. demonstrate its application to federated boosted trees, including the trade-off between privacy and predictive utility [16]. PrivateBoost's additive aggregation interface could support bounded contributions and calibrated noise, with privacy accounting covering both feature-statistics estimation and subsequent training releases. Protection against the aggregator would require perturbing aggregates before it observes them. Such an extension would need to account for repeated participation and evaluate the resulting effects on predictive performance.

Protecting against malicious clients requires additional checks before aggregation. Prio uses secret-shared non-interactive proofs to verify that submitted data satisfy specified validity constraints without revealing individual values [38]. Similar checks could enforce bounds on gradient and Hessian contributions and constraints on histogram structure, limiting manipulation through oversized or malformed submissions. Remote attestation provides a complementary basis for assessing client software integrity [39]. If contribution generation runs within an attested protected environment and its outputs are bound to the submitted shares, this could help enforce the prescribed computation. Neither approach establishes that the underlying records are truthful: deliberately misleading contributions within the permitted constraints would remain possible. These mechanisms are not part of the current implementation.

Infrastructure trust and participation metadata require separate consideration. The security analysis assumes honest-but-curious behaviour and excludes mixed coalitions, including collaboration between shareholders and the aggregator. Independent operation can support that separation, but does not enforce it cryptographically. Fresh round commitments also do not conceal network addresses, submission timing or persistent pseudonyms visible to shareholders. Anonymous communication could reduce some of this linkability, depending on the deployment. The designated shareholder organisations and their responsibilities can be specified before enrolment, while the applicable consent and data-governance arrangements depend on the deployment and jurisdiction.

Beyond the evaluated learner, the aggregation interface applies to training procedures expressed through additive per-record statistics. Histogram construction in LightGBM and the leaf-averaging step in CatBoost's Plain-mode split evaluation provide related examples [40, 41], while formulations of first-order boosting also use additive statistics [42]. Supporting a complete learning algorithm requires examining its other operations: ordered categorical statistics, prefix-dependent ordered boosting, residual quantiles and selection based on individual gradient magnitudes are not supplied by the present interface. Tree-growth policies also change the balance between the number of aggregation rounds and the work performed in each round. These differences should guide extensions rather than assuming that compatibility with histogram aggregation establishes compatibility with the entire learner.

Tabular foundation models provide a further point of comparison. TabPFN achieved strong predictive performance on benchmarks with up to 10,000 samples and 500 features [43], but its published inference procedure uses individual labelled training examples as context. PrivateBoost's aggregation interface exposes sums of per-record statistics, so it cannot directly support that procedure. Applying comparable privacy protection to prior-data fitted networks would require a different computational design [44].

The findings support a design in which personal devices perform brief local computations while infrastructure parties coordinate aggregation. The next evaluations should examine independently connected single-record clients under realistic participation patterns and measure the costs of stronger output privacy and contribution validation. Together, these would clarify the deployment settings in which the demonstrated mobile feasibility can translate into sustained training at larger scales.

Conclusion

PrivateBoost enables federated gradient boosting from individual records without requiring clients to fit local models or coordinate with one another. Its fixedshareholder architecture combines secret-shared contributions with a client workload that remains independent of the participant population for a given model and shareholder configuration. Simulations across four medical datasets show predictive performance comparable to matched centralised training and resilience to randomly sampled client dropout.

The physical pilot demonstrates that consumer smartphones and tablets holding batches of records can complete training unattended through operating-systemmanaged background execution, with median share-generation times of 0.3-1.0 milliseconds per round. Together, these results establish a practical foundation for learning from records distributed across personal devices. By placing aggregation coordination on infrastructure parties, PrivateBoost allows participation to fit around intermittent device availability, bringing collaborative medical learning closer to the settings in which individuals hold and contribute their own data. Indicators [36] (ID 891, DOI 10.24432/C53919), from which the class-balanced 70,692record subset analysed here is produced by the preparation script in the code repository. For Pima Indians Diabetes, the preparation script uses the CSV mirror maintained by Jason Brownlee [35]; the original study is described by Smith et al. [34].

No new patient data were collected: the real-world deployment partitioned these same public datasets across the participating devices. Deployment telemetry was collected in a cloud document database (Google Firestore) operated by the authors, and account and device identifiers were stripped before analysis. The datasets, training-run outputs and de-identified deployment records are publicly available with the analysis code on Zenodo (DOI https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24354793), and figure source data are provided with this paper in the Source Data.xlsx workbook.

Fig 1: Institution-centric versus patient-level federated learning with PrivateBoost. (a) In the conventional cross-silo setting, patients provide data to institutions, which perform local training and share model updates. Each institution has access to the records within its cohort. (b) In PrivateBoost, individual patients can participate directly: each client holds a single record and distributes secret shares to a fixed set of shareholders. Shareholders aggregate shared statistics rather than raw records; protection depends on the stated collusion assumptions and does not exclude inference from released aggregates.

the client's tree pathbut not the bin: every submission covers all bins of all features + 2 logical bins, including overflow bins.

The current implementation allocates B slots = B + 3 histogram entries per feature, using the boundary-array length; the final entry is unused for finite feature values. Write A = T t=1 d-1 ℓ=0 |V t,ℓ | for the total number of active-node processing steps, with A ≤ T (2 d -1). In the base protocol, each single-record client submits a dense gradient-Hessian histogram for at most one node per tree-building iteration. Client-to-shareholder histogram traffic is therefore O(T dF B slots cn) field elements. With path hiding, each client submits for every active node, giving an upper bound of O(AF B slots cn). The one-time statistics phase adds O(F cn) field elements. For each active node with sufficient aggregate shares, the selected m shareholders return summed histogram shares, giving at most O(AF B slots m) field elements over training. Split decisions are made separately for each node with an eligible split. Sharing each secret requires evaluating a degree-(m -1) polynomial at n points. Per-client sharing work is O(T dF B slots nm) in the base protocol and at most O(AF B slots nm) with path hiding. Shareholders add incoming shares position-wise. The implementation computes Lagrange coefficients once per reconstructed vector, costing O(m 2 ) field operations, and then uses them for its O(F B slots ) entries. Aggregate reconstruction therefore costs O(A(m 2 + F B slots m)), with a further O(AF B slots ) for split finding.
